title: Repeating Things (While Loops)
story: You're counting down to a rocket launch: 10, 9, 8, 7... The same action — saying one number — repeats over and over until the count reaches zero. Then: LIFTOFF! Computers are amazing at this kind of repetitive work.
why: Programs often need to repeat actions: printing every name on a list, counting down a timer, running a game loop until the player quits. `while` loops make repetition easy — write the code once, run it as many times as you need.
analogy: A while-loop is like a merry-go-round — it keeps spinning while the music plays (the condition is true), and stops the moment the music ends (the condition becomes false).
try_it: Change the countdown to start from 10 instead of 5. Then try counting UP instead of down — start at 1 and count to 10. What condition do you need? What does `count = count + 1` do inside the loop?
tips: Use `var` (not `let`) for variables that need to change inside a loop — `let` variables are locked forever.
Always make sure something inside the loop changes the condition — otherwise you'll loop forever.
The condition is checked BEFORE each time through the loop. If it's false on the very first check, the loop body runs zero times.
You can put `if`/`else` inside a loop, and you can put loops inside `if`/`else` — they work together.
common_mistakes: Using `let` instead of `var` for a loop counter: `let count = 5;` then `count = count - 1;` — this won't work because `let` variables can't change.
Forgetting to update the counter: the condition never becomes false, so the loop runs forever.
Putting a semicolon after the while condition: `while count > 0; {` — the semicolon creates an empty loop body.
Using `<=` when you meant `<`: `while count < 0` runs zero times if count starts at 5, because 5 is not less than 0.
